# Rheumatoid arthritis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Joint diseases > Rheumatoid arthritis*

[Original Article Link](/library/-f0DK2)

---

## Summary

Rheumatoid <u>arthritis</u> (<u>RA</u>) is a chronic, systemic, inflammatory autoimmune disorder that primarily affects the <u>joints</u> (e.g., causes <u>pain</u>, swelling, synovial destruction, deformities), but may also manifest with extraarticular features (e.g., <u>rheumatoid nodules</u>, <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>). The risk of <u>RA</u> increases with age, and the disease predominantly affects women. The diagnosis is clinical and may be supported by laboratory tests (e.g., <u>rheumatoid factor</u>, <u>anticitrullinated peptide antibodies</u>) and imaging studies (e.g., the presence of <u>synovitis</u> on <u>ultrasound</u> and, later in the disease course, bone <u>erosions</u> and/or <u>joint</u> space narrowing on <u>x-rays</u>). There is no curative therapy for <u>RA</u> but early intervention with <u>disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs</u> (<u>DMARDs</u>) using a treat-to-target strategy can prevent disease progression and <u>RA</u>-related disability.

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>

* ∼ 0.24% worldwide [[1]](/library/BIXzUz)

* 1% in northern Europe and US [[2]](/library/yIXd2z)

* Sex: : <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (3:1) [[3]](/library/4Na3YO)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: : 30–50 years  [[4]](/library/oOd0tJ0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Idiopathic</u> inflammatory autoimmune disorder of unknown etiology

* <u>Risk factors</u> include: [[5]](/library/mNaVbO)

* Genetic disposition: associated with <u>HLA-DR4</u> and <u>HLA</u>-DR1 [[6]](/library/r-afAM)

* Environmental factors (e.g., smoking)

* <u>Female sex hormones</u>: Risk of <u>RA</u> is increased in <u>premenopausal</u> individuals and in the first year postpartum.

* Infection (e.g., <u>periodontitis</u>) [[7]](/library/eacxja0)

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Family history</u> of <u>RA</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “A DRone with 4 propellers and 1 camera:” rheumatoid <u>arthritis</u> is associated with <u>HLA</u>-DR4 and <u>HLA</u>-DR1.

---

## Pathophysiology

* Certain <u>interstitial</u> tissue <u>proteins</u> (e.g. intracellular filament protein <u>vimentin</u>, <u>filaggrin</u>, <u>type II collagen</u>) undergo a <u>posttranslational modification</u> that involves the conversion of <u>arginine</u> to <u>citrulline</u> (<u>citrullination</u>). [[8]](/library/q6YCNJ)

* <u>Citrullinated</u> <u>proteins</u> are recognized as foreign by the <u>antigen-presenting cells</u> that present them to <u>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells</u>.

* Activation of <u>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells</u> leads to the following sequences of events: [[9]](/library/I6YYmJ)

* <u>IL-4</u> production → <u>B-cell</u> <u>proliferation</u> and differentiation → production of <u>anticitrullinated peptide antibodies</u> → <u>type II hypersensitivity reaction</u> and <u>type III hypersensitivity reaction</u>

* Migration of <u>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells</u> to <u>synovial joints</u> → secretion of <u>cytokines</u> (<u>IFN-γ</u>, <u>IL-17</u>) → recruitment of <u>macrophages</u> → secretion of <u>cytokines</u> (<u>TNF-α</u>, <u>IL-1</u>, <u>IL-6</u>) → inflammation and <u>proliferation</u>

* Bouts of inflammation, <u>angiogenesis</u>, and <u>proliferation</u> → proliferative <u>granulation tissue</u> with mononuclear inflammatory cells → <u>pannus</u> and synovial <u>hypertrophy</u> → invasion, progressive destruction, and deterioration of <u>cartilage</u> and bone

* <u>Antibodies</u> against <u>Fc</u> portion of <u>IgG</u> (<u>rheumatoid factor</u>, RF) are produced to aid in removing <u>autoantibodies</u> and <u>immune complexes</u>.

* RF excess triggers formation of new <u>immune complexes</u> and <u>type III HSR</u>

* Individuals with positive RF are more likely to develop extraarticular manifestations. [[10]](/library/7-a4AM)





![Schematic representation of the pathophysiology of rheumatoid arthritis](media/mi7lem5co99zx22h1fhttikp.jpg)

## Clinical features

### Articular manifestations [[11]](/library/45a34O)




* Polyarthralgia

* Symmetrical <u>pain</u> and swelling of affected <u>joints</u> (also at rest)

* Frequently affected <u>joints</u> ;   [[12]](/library/TYa6oQ)

* <u>Metacarpophalangeal</u> <u>joints</u> (<u>MCP joints</u>)

* <u>Proximal</u> interphalangeal <u>joints</u> (<u>PIP</u> <u>joints</u>)

* <u>Wrist joints</u>

* <u>Knee joints</u>

* <u>Metatarsophalangeal joints</u> (<u>MTP joints</u>)

* Rarely affected: <u>distal interphalangeal joints</u> (<u>DIP</u> <u>joints</u>), first carpometacarpal (<u>CMC</u>) <u>joint</u>, and the <u>axial skeleton</u> (except for the <u>cervical spine</u>)

* Morning stiffness (often > 30 min) that usually improves with activity

* <u>Joint</u> deformities

* Rheumatoid hand is characteristic and typically manifests with one or more of the following deformities:  

* Deepening of the interosseous spaces of the dorsum of hand

* Swan neck deformity: <u>PIP</u> hyperextension and <u>DIP</u> <u>flexion</u>

* Boutonniere deformity: <u>PIP</u> <u>flexion</u> and <u>DIP</u> hyperextension.

* Hitchhiker thumb deformity (Z deformity of the thumb): hyperextension of the <u>interphalangeal joint</u> with fixed <u>flexion</u> of the <u>MCP joint</u> [[13]](/library/O5aI4O)

* Ulnar deviation of the fingers

* Piano key sign: <u>dorsal</u> subluxation of the <u>ulna</u>

* <u>Hammer toe</u> or <u>claw toe</u>

* <u>Atlantoaxial subluxation</u> (see “<u>Rheumatoid arthritis of the cervical spine</u>” below)

* <u>Physical examination</u>: compression test (<u>Gaenslen squeeze test</u>) 

* Painful compression of hands (or feet) at the level of the <u>MCP joint</u> (<u>metatarsophalangeal joint</u>)

* Painful handshake is an early sign of <u>arthritis</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>DIP</u> <u>joints</u> are not typically affected in <u>RA</u>.

### Extraarticular manifestations [[14]](/library/L5awkO)




* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* Low-grade <u>fever</u>

* <u>Myalgia</u>

* <u>Malaise</u>

* Fatigue

* Weight loss

* Night sweats

* Rheumatoid nodules

* <u>Skin</u>

* Nontender, firm, subcutaneous swellings (2 mm–5 cm)

* Commonly occur in areas exposed to higher pressure, e.g., extensor side of the forearm, bony prominences

* <u>Lungs</u>

* Typically bilateral and peripheral

* Rheumatoid pulmonary <u>nodules</u> may be accompanied by <u>fibrosis</u> and <u>pneumoconiosis</u> (<u>Caplan syndrome</u>).

* <u>Lungs</u>

* <u>Pleuritis</u>, <u>pleural effusions</u>

* <u>Interstitial lung disease</u> (e.g., organizing <u>pneumonia</u>) [[15]](/library/M5aMkO)

* <u>Eye</u>: <u>keratoconjunctivitis sicca</u>, <u>scleritis</u>, and <u>episcleritis</u>  [[16]](/library/-EbDyv)

* Endocrine and <u>exocrine glands</u>: secondary <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>

* Hematological

* <u>Anemia</u>

* <u>Anemia of chronic disease</u> (<u>normocytic anemia</u>)

* <u>NSAIDs</u> and/or <u>steroids</u> → increased risk of <u>GI bleeding</u> → <u>iron deficiency anemia</u> (<u>microcytic anemia</u>)

* <u>Methotrexate</u> → decreased <u>folate</u> level → <u>macrocytic anemia</u>

* <u>Neutropenia</u>

* <u>Splenomegaly</u>

* <u>Large granular lymphocyte leukemia</u>

* <u>Lymphoma</u>

* Musculoskeletal

* <u>Tenosynovitis</u> and <u>bursitis</u>

* <u>Carpal tunnel syndrome</u>

* Typical nocturnal <u>paresthesia</u> of <u>volar</u> hand, thumb, index and middle fingers

* <u>Atrophy</u> of <u>thenar muscles</u> → difficulty making a fist and inability to oppose the thumb

* <u>Tarsal tunnel syndrome</u>

* <u>Heart</u>

* <u>Pericarditis</u> and <u>myocarditis</u>

* Increased risk of <u>myocardial infarction</u>, <u>stroke</u>, <u>CHF</u>, and <u>atrial fibrillation</u>  [[17]](/library/zEbryv)

* Vascular

* Peripheral <u>vasculitis</u>, manifests as <u>livedo reticularis</u>

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* <u>Purpura</u>

* <u>Vasculitic</u> <u>ulcers</u>

* Necrosing fingertips

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

## Pathology

* Synovial pannus formation and bone invasion: pathological layer of proliferative <u>granulation tissue</u>, mononuclear inflammatory cells, and <u>fibroblast</u>-like <u>mesenchymal</u> cells, releasing <u>cytokines</u> and enzymes, which, in turn, damage and invade the surrounding <u>connective tissue</u>  [[18]](/library/TiY6IK)

* Synovial lining <u>hyperplasia</u> with <u>mononuclear cell</u> infiltrate

* Perivascular inflammatory infiltrates

* <u>Angiogenesis</u>

* <u>Fibrin</u> deposition on synovial surfaces

* <u>Rheumatoid nodules</u>: central <u>fibrinoid necrosis</u> with palisading <u>histiocytes</u> (<u>epithelioid cells</u>)





![Rheumatoid nodule](media/iw3clg8ieyqm4ztxxrje77bl.jpg)

Rheumatoid nodule

## Subtypes and variants

### Rheumatoid arthritis of the cervical spine [[12]](/library/TYa6oQ)




<u>RA</u> typically affects the <u>cervical spine</u> early in the course of the disease, while normally sparing the thoracic and <u>lumbar spine</u>. <u>RA of the cervical spine</u> most commonly manifests with <u>atlantoaxial subluxation</u>. Other patterns of instability are atlantoaxial impaction and subaxial subluxation.




#### Atlantoaxial subluxation




* Definition: a potentially life-threatening complication caused by the inflammatory destruction of the <u>ligaments</u> affecting the <u>atlantoaxial joint</u> and the <u>intervertebral joints</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> and stiffness of the neck (typically early-morning <u>neck pain</u> at rest)

* Head tilt

* Neurological deficits

* <u>Cervical radiculopathy</u> with peripheral <u>paresthesias</u> of the upper limb

* In some cases, symptoms of high <u>spinal cord compression</u> (see also “<u>Incomplete spinal cord injury</u>”)

* Slowly progressive <u>spastic</u> quadriparesis

* <u>Hyperreflexia</u> or positive <u>Babinski reflex</u>

* <u>Respiratory insufficiency</u>

* Diagnostics

* Extension and <u>flexion</u> <u>x-rays</u> of the <u>cervical spine</u>

* <u>MRI</u>

* Treatment: <u>surgery</u> if instability or <u>myelopathy</u> are present





> [!TIP]
> Before undergoing <u>general anesthesia</u>, an <u>airway</u> and neck assessment is crucial in patients with <u>RA</u>, as <u>atlantoaxial subluxation</u> may be present, which increases the risk for <u>spinal cord injury</u>. Preoperative <u>flexion</u>-extension radiographs can help to evaluate the position of the <u>cervical vertebra</u> <u>atlas</u> (C1) with regard to the axis (C2).




### Felty syndrome [[12]](/library/TYa6oQ)




* Definition: a severe subtype of <u>RA</u> characterized by <u>neutropenia</u> and <u>splenomegaly</u> .

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: rare (1–3 % of patients with <u>RA</u>) [[19]](/library/U30b3f)

* Clinical features

* Clinical triad consisting of <u>arthritis</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>, and <u>neutropenia</u>

* Other features

* <u>Skin ulcers</u> of the lower limbs (indicating <u>vasculitis</u>)

* <u>Hepatomegaly</u>

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Chest pain</u> (indicating <u>pleuritis</u> or <u>pericarditis</u>)

* Associated with increased risk of <u>non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Leukopenia</u> with selective <u>neutropenia</u>

* ↑ RF

* ↑ <u>ACPA</u>

* Treatment

* <u>DMARD</u>: <u>methotrexate</u>

* Alternative: <u>rituximab</u>  [[20]](/library/KOdUtJ0)

* Prompt and aggressive <u>antibiotic</u> treatment for suspected infections

* Consider <u>splenectomy</u> to treat <u>leukopenia</u> and improve the disease course.

* <u>G-CSF</u> (<u>granulocyte-colony</u> stimulating factor) in cases of severe <u>granulocytopenia</u>

* Complications: <u>Neutropenia</u> increases risk of recurrent bacterial infections.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Arthritis</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>, and <u>neutropenia</u> may suggest <u>Felty syndrome</u>.




### Undifferentiated arthritis [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[21]](/library/V-aGwM)[[22]](/library/KTcU7b0)




* Definition: symptoms of inflammatory <u>arthritis</u> that are not attributable to trauma or acute inflammatory events; often a transitional state preceding a definitive diagnosis  [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[22]](/library/KTcU7b0)

* Approach to management

* Refer to a rheumatologist for periodical follow-up.

* Management strategies are aimed at preventing progression and can be:

* Nonpharmacological: e.g., <u>smoking cessation</u>, <u>oral health programs</u> [[7]](/library/eacxja0)

* Pharmacological: <u>DMARDs</u>  [[23]](/library/wTchGb0)

* Prognosis [[23]](/library/wTchGb0)

* Spontaneous remission in approx. 50% of patients

* <u>RA</u> develops in approx. one-third of patients  [[21]](/library/V-aGwM)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[24]](/library/s5atlO)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)




* The diagnosis of <u>RA</u> is clinical. 

* Consider <u>RA</u> in patients with <u>arthralgia</u>, <u>joint</u> stiffness, and <u>synovitis</u> lasting ≥ 6 weeks (see “Clinical features”).

* Consider alternative diagnoses in patients with atypical presentations (see “Differential diagnoses”).

* Perform diagnostic studies to further support the diagnosis and help establish disease severity.

* Routine laboratory tests.  [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)

* <u>X-ray</u> as the initial imaging study

* Consult rheumatology, particularly if the diagnosis is uncertain and when choosing a treatment regimen.





> [!TIP]
> <u>RA</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. The <u>2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for RA</u> can help identify <u>RA</u>, but the criteria do not need to be fulfilled in order to establish a diagnosis. [[24]](/library/s5atlO)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)




#### Routine studies




* Nonspecific parameters 

* ↑ Inflammatory markers

* ↑ <u>CRP</u> and ↑ <u>ESR</u>

* Other <u>acute phase reactants</u> may also be elevated (e.g., <u>ferritin</u>).

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>anemia of chronic disease</u>, <u>thrombocytosis</u>

* <u>TFTs</u>: to rule out an <u>autoimmune thyroid disease</u>, which is common in patients with <u>RA</u>

* <u>Serology</u>: ↑ <u>ANAs</u> in 30–50% of patients with <u>RA</u> [[21]](/library/V-aGwM)

* Specific parameters (<u>serological studies</u>)  [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[26]](/library/z2br4G)

* Anticitrullinated peptide antibodies;  (<u>ACPA</u>), e.g., anticyclic <u>citrullinated</u> <u>peptide</u> (<u>anti-CCP</u>)  [[27]](/library/ncc71Y0)

* Rheumatoid factor;  (RF): <u>IgM</u> <u>autoantibodies</u> against the <u>Fc region</u> of <u>IgG antibodies</u>  [[21]](/library/V-aGwM)

* <u>Serological studies</u> may be negative (i.e., <u>seronegative RA</u>)





| <br>Serological testing in rheumatoid arthritis [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[21]](/library/V-aGwM)[[26]](/library/z2br4G)[[28]](/library/ch1a1g0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Sensitivity</u> | <u>Specificity</u> | Other |
| <u>ACPA</u> | <br>* ∼ 70%<br><br> | <br>* > 90%<br><br> | <br>* Positive test associated with an aggressive disease course<br><br> |
| RF | <br>* 80–86%<br><br> | <br><br>* Positive test associated with an aggressive disease course<br><br>* Elevated RF is not <u>pathognomonic</u> of <u>RA</u> (may also be elevated in infectious diseases, other autoimmune diseases, and even healthy individuals)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>ANA</u> | <br>* 30–50%<br><br> | <br>* 85%<br><br> | <br>* Typically elevated in <u>connective tissue disorders</u>, may also be found in <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u> and <u>vasculitides</u><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Approx. 30% of patients with <u>RA</u> are negative for <u>ACPA</u> and RF. [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)




![Structure of IgM and IgG rheumatoid factor](media/n13v1v2a458kqat6y77g9v6x.jpg)

Structure of IgM and IgG rheumatoid factor




#### Additional studies




Additional studies should be considered on an individual basis.




* <u>Synovial fluid analysis</u>: not routinely recommended [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)

* Indications

* Suspicion of <u>septic arthritis</u>

* Atypical presentation, to rule out differential diagnoses (e.g., <u>gout</u>)

* Findings are nonspecific [[21]](/library/V-aGwM)

* Cloudy, yellow appearance

* Sterile specimen with <u>leukocytosis</u> (<u>WBC count</u> 5,000–50,000 /μL)

* ↑ <u>Neutrophils</u>, <u>granulocytes</u>, and ragocytes

* ↑ Protein level

* Possibly RF

* <u>ASCVD risk assessment</u>  [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)

* Recommended in all patients with <u>RA</u>, as <u>RA</u> is an <u>ASCVD risk-enhancing factor</u>

* Includes <u>diabetes mellitus screening</u>, <u>screening for lipid disorders</u>, and a risk calculation using the <u>2013 ACC/AHA pooled cohort equation</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>ASCVD</u> is the most common cause of premature <u>death</u> in patients with <u>RA</u>; therefore, an <u>ASCVD risk assessment</u> is recommended in all patients with <u>RA</u>.




### Imaging studies [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[29]](/library/L4XwPy)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)




While <u>x-ray</u> is recommended as the initial test, <u>ultrasound</u> and <u>MRI</u> might additionally be necessary to assess <u>joint</u> disease severity.




* <u>X-ray</u>:  initial test

* Studies

* Baseline radiographs of both hands (dorsopalmar view) and feet

* Radiographs of symptomatic <u>joints</u>

* Findings 

* Early: <u>soft tissue</u> swelling, <u>osteopenia</u> (juxtaarticular)

* Late: <u>joint</u> space narrowing, marginal <u>erosions</u> of <u>cartilage</u> and bone, <u>osteopenia</u> (generalized), <u>subchondral cysts</u>

* <u>Ultrasound</u>   [[31]](/library/fackPa0)

* Indication: If available, perform on affected <u>joints</u> to detect clinical or subclinical <u>synovitis</u>.

* Supportive findings

* Early signs of inflammation: e.g., subclinical <u>synovitis</u> (synovial <u>hyperemia</u>)

* Synovial <u>proliferation</u> (<u>pannus</u> formation)

* Joint effusion: increased fluid (e.g., <u>pus</u>, blood, inflammatory infiltrate) within the synovial compartment of a <u>joint</u>

* Using contrast can increase the <u>sensitivity</u> of detecting inflammation.

* <u>MRI</u> of the affected <u>joints</u> (with or without contrast) 

* Can help detect early changes in <u>large joints</u> (e.g., subclinical <u>synovitis</u>)

* Consider especially if <u>cervical spine</u> involvement is suspected (see “<u>Atlantoaxial subluxation</u>”).

* Further imaging studies: Perform if extraarticular manifestations are suspected (e.g., a <u>CT scan</u> for <u>interstitial lung disease</u>, an <u>echocardiogram</u> for <u>pericarditis</u>).





> [!TIP]
> Typical <u>RA</u> findings on <u>x-rays</u> may be subtle or absent upon diagnosis in many patients with early <u>RA</u>; therefore, <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> may be more informative, as they have higher <u>sensitivity</u> for detecting early signs of inflammation and <u>erosion</u>.

## Differential diagnoses

| <br>Common causes of chronic arthropathy <br> |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Condition | Rheumatoid <u>arthritis</u> (<u>RA</u>) | <u>Osteoarthritis</u> | <u>Psoriatic arthritis</u> | <u>Gout</u> | <u>Pseudogout</u> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br>* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u><br><br>* Age (> 55 years)<br><br><br> | <br>* Sex: <u>♀</u> = <u>♂</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Sex: <u>♀</u> < <u>♂</u><br><br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 30–60 years<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Sex: ∼ <u>♀</u> = <u>♂</u><br><br>* Majority of people > 50 years<br><br><br> |
| <u>Risk factors</u> | <br>* <u>Family history</u> of <u>RA</u><br><br> | <br><br>* History of <u>joint</u> injury or trauma<br><br>* <u>Obese</u> patients<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Family or personal history of <u>psoriasis</u><br><br>* May be triggered by trauma or infections (e.g., <u>HIV infection</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Family history</u> of <u>gout</u><br><br>* <u>Heavy drinking</u><br><br><br> | <br>* History of <u>joint</u> trauma, familial <u>chondrocalcinosis</u>, <u>hyperparathyroidism</u><br><br> |
| Course of disease | <br>* Chronic course with varied patterns<br><br>* Monocyclic<br><br>* Polycyclic<br><br>* Progressive<br><br> | <br>* Chronic, progressive course<br><br> | <br>* Chronic, progressive course<br><br> | <br>* Chronic course with acute attacks<br><br> |  |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u> (e.g., fatigue, <u>fever</u>)<br><br>* Morning stiffness > 30 minutes<br><br>* <u>Pain</u>/stiffness may be relieved by activity<br><br>* Articular inflammation (swollen, warm <u>joints</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* No <u>constitutional symptoms</u><br><br>* Morning stiffness < 30 minutes<br><br>* <u>Pain</u>/stiffness worsens with increased activity and relieved by rest<br><br>* Noninflammatory<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Psoriatic <u>skin</u> lesions and <u>nail</u> changes<br><br>* <u>Dactylitis</u> (<u>sausage fingers</u>)<br><br>* <u>Enthesitis</u>: inflammation of the <u>enthesis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Articular inflammation (swollen, <u>erythematous</u>, warm <u>joints</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* Eventually development of <u>tophi</u><br><br> | <br>* Chronic inflammatory <u>arthritis</u> in <u>pseudogout</u> is rare and resembles <u>RA</u> (e.g., morning stiffness, <u>constitutional symptoms</u>)<br><br> |  |  |  |  |
| Symmetry of <u>joint</u> involvement | <br>* Symmetrical<br><br> | <br>* Usually asymmetrical<br><br> | <br><br>* Asymmetrical oligoarticular type<br><br>* Symmetrical <u>polyarthritis</u> type<br><br><br> | <br>* Asymmetrical<br><br> |  |
| Pattern of disease | <br><br>* <u>Polyarthritis</u>: predominantly wrists, <u>MCP</u>, and <u>PIP</u> <u>joints</u><br><br>* Spares <u>DIP</u> <u>joints</u> and first <u>CMC joint</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Polyarthritis</u><br><br>* Predominantly <u>weight-bearing</u> <u>joints</u> (e.g., hip and knees)<br><br>* <u>PIP</u> and <u>DIP</u> <u>joints</u> (<u>Bouchard nodes</u> and <u>Heberden nodes</u> respectively)<br><br>* First <u>CMC joint</u><br><br>* Spares the wrist and the <u>MCP joints</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Polyarthritis</u> or <u>oligoarthritis</u><br><br>* Commonly <u>DIP</u> <u>joint</u> and/or spinal involvement<br><br>* Sometimes <u>large joint</u> involvement<br><br> | <br>* Usually <u>monoarthritis</u>: typical locations include the big toe (<u>MTP joint</u>), knee<br>and thumb (<u>MCP joint</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Monoarthritis</u> (rarely <u>oligoarthritis</u>): commonly knee and <u>wrist joints</u><br><br> |
| Laboratory findings | <br><br>* Blood: RF, <u>ACPA</u><br><br>* <u>Synovial fluid</u><br><br>* <u>WBC</u>: 5,000–50,000 /μL<br><br>* ↑ <u>Neutrophils</u>, <u>phagocytes</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Proteins</u><br><br>* ↓ Viscosity<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Synovial fluid</u><br>* <u>WBC</u>: < 2,000/Î¼L (noninflammatory)<br><br> | <br>* No specific laboratory features<br><br> | <br><br>* Blood: ↑ <u>uric acid</u><br><br>* <u>Synovial fluid</u>: negatively <u>birefringent</u> needle-shaped crystals<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Synovial fluid</u>: positively <u>birefringent</u> rhomboid crystals<br><br> |
| Imaging | <br><br>* <u>Joint</u> space narrowing<br><br>* <u>Erosions</u><br><br>* <u>Subchondral cysts</u><br><br>* Juxtaarticular demineralization<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Joint</u> space narrowing<br><br>* <u>Osteophytes</u><br><br>* <u>Subchondral sclerosis</u><br><br>* Subchondral bone cysts<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Combination of <u>joint</u> <u>erosion</u> and bone growth<br><br>* <u>Pencil-in-cup</u> deformity of the <u>joints</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Rat-bite <u>erosions</u> (<u>erosions</u> with overhanging <u>cortical bone</u>) in advanced cases<br><br> | <br>* <u>Chondrocalcinosis</u><br><br> |




* Other differential diagnoses

* Autoimmune-related <u>arthritis</u> (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>SLE</u>, <u>rheumatic fever</u>, <u>mixed connective tissue disease</u>, <u>polymyalgia rheumatica</u>)

* <u>Enteropathic arthritis</u>

* <u>Vasculitides</u>

* <u>Hemochromatosis</u>

* <u>Viral arthritis</u> (e.g., <u>parvovirus B19</u>, <u>hepatitis</u> <u>viruses</u>)

* <u>Lyme arthritis</u>

* <u>Reactive arthritis</u> (post-<u>urethritis</u>, post-enteritis)

* <u>Juvenile idiopathic arthritis</u>

* <u>CPPD disease</u>

* <u>Basic calcium phosphate crystal deposition diseases</u>

* <u>Fibromyalgia</u>

* <u>Soft tissue</u> rheumatic disorders: a group of common nonsystemic focal syndromes characterized by nonarticular <u>pain</u>

* <u>Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy</u>: typically characterized by <u>periosteal reaction</u> in the <u>metaphyses</u> and <u>diaphyses</u> of <u>long bones</u> and associated with <u>lung</u> disease (e.g., <u>lung cancer</u>)

* Palindromic rheumatism: autoinflammatory and autoimmune disorder [[34]](/library/Qldu9J0)

* Characterized by relapsing episodes of <u>joint</u> <u>pain</u>, swelling, and stiffness that typically last 12–72 hours followed by asymptomatic periods lasting days to months

* May progress to <u>RA</u> or other autoimmune conditions (e.g., <u>SLE</u>)

## Treatment

### Approach [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




* Initiate acute antiinflammatory treatment with <u>glucocorticoids</u> and <u>NSAIDs</u> for disease flares.

* Long-term treatment

* Initiate treatment with <u>conventional DMARD</u> monotherapy.

* Consider short-term concomitant antiinflammatory treatment.

* Initiate nonpharmacological management.

* Consider surgical treatment in specific cases (e.g., patients with severe <u>joint</u> deformities).





> [!TIP]
> Consult a rheumatologist before initiating treatment.




### Acute antiinflammatory treatment [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




Temporary (< 3 months) symptomatic treatment with <u>glucocorticoids</u> and/or <u>NSAIDs</u> is indicated for disease flares (i.e., episodes of increased disease activity and symptom worsening).  [[36]](/library/ibcJta0)




* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>

* Systemic <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE

* Short-term (i.e., < 3 months) therapy at the lowest effective dose is preferred.

* Longer-term therapy: Only use in patients with highly active <u>RA</u> who do not respond to maximum doses of <u>DMARDs</u>.  [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)

* See also “<u>Side effects of glucocorticoid therapy</u>” and “Preventing complications of long-term <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy” in “<u>Glucocorticoids</u>.”

* Intraarticular injections (e.g., with <u>triamcinolone</u> acetonide) can be considered by specialists alongside treatment with <u>DMARDs</u> in patients with predominant symptoms in ≥ 1 medium or <u>large joint</u>.

* <u>NSAIDs</u> and <u>selective COX-2 inhibitors</u>: : relieve symptoms, but do not improve the prognosis 

* <u>Ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Diclofenac</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Celecoxib</u> DOSAGE

* Other measures: If a flare occurs due to medication tapering, restart the previous effective treatment regimen.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Glucocorticoids</u> should be used at the lowest effective dose and only for short periods of time to reduce the risk of their many adverse effects (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>, infections). [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




### Long-term pharmacological treatment  [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




#### Initiation of treatment




* All patients (regardless of baseline disease activity or disease duration): monotherapy with a <u>conventional DMARD</u>

* Consider short-term concomitant use of acute antiinflammatory therapy (i.e., <u>glucocorticoids</u> and/or <u>NSAIDs</u>) for symptom control until the onset of action of <u>DMARDs</u> (e.g., ≥ 6 weeks). [[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)





> [!TIP]
> Early administration of <u>DMARDs</u> improves patients' outcomes.




#### Treat-to-target strategy [[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




Long-term treatment is guided by <u>disease activity scoring systems for RA</u> involving clinical and laboratory features, e.g., <u>CDAI</u>. The 2021 <u>ACR</u> guideline does not provide definitions for different stages of disease activity.




* Target at 3 months: ≥ 50% improvement in the disease activity index

* Target at 6 months: low disease activity (or remission)

* Targets not reached: Consult rheumatology to adjust treatment.





> [!TIP]
> A treat-to-target strategy can prevent <u>RA</u>-related disability. [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not discontinue all <u>DMARDs</u> in patients who achieve disease remission, as this may trigger a disease flare. [[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




#### Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (<u>DMARDs</u>) [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




<u>DMARDs</u> are used as long-term therapy; . They interfere with the inflammatory mechanisms of <u>RA</u>, which can potentially lead to remission. <u>DMARD</u> therapy reduces <u>RA</u> mortality and <u>morbidity</u> by up to 30%. Prevention and monitoring of potential adverse effects are required (see also “Adverse effects” in “<u>Immunosuppressants</u>”).  [[12]](/library/TYa6oQ)




##### Synthetic <u>DMARDs</u>




| <br>Synthetic <u>DMARDs</u> for <u>RA</u> [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drug class | Agent | Important considerations |
| <br>Conventional DMARDs<br> | <br>* <u>Methotrexate</u> (<u>MTX</u>) DOSAGE: first-line treatment in patients with moderate to high disease activity  [[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)<br><br> | <br><br>* Adverse effects [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)<br><br>* <u>Stomatitis</u><br><br>* <u>Pancytopenia</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>AST</u>, <u>ALT</u><br><br>* <u>Teratogenicity</u><br><br>* <u>Pneumonitis</u><br><br>* To minimize adverse effects, administer <u>folic acid</u>. DOSAGE. [[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br>* Avoid administering <u>NSAIDs</u> on the same day as <u>MTX</u>.<br><br><br> |

[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br> | <br>* Adverse effects [[7]](/library/eacxja0)<br><br>* <u>Hyperpigmentation</u><br><br>* <u>Retinopathy</u>  [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br>* Severe <u>rash</u><br><br> |  |

[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br> | <br>* Adverse effects [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br>* <u>Diarrhea</u><br><br>* <u>Agranulocytosis</u><br><br>* Cutaneous <u>hypersensitivity reactions</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Leflunomide DOSAGE: Consider if all other <u>conventional DMARDs</u> are contraindicated. [[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br>* Mechanism of action: reversibly inhibits <u>dihydroorotate</u> <u>dehydrogenase</u> → impaired <u>pyrimidine</u> synthesis → inhibition of <u>T-cell</u> <u>proliferation</u><br><br>* Other indications: <u>psoriatic arthritis</u><br><br> | <br>* Adverse effects<br><br>* <u>High blood pressure</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>AST</u>, <u>ALT</u><br><br>* <u>Teratogenicity</u><br><br>* GI symptoms (e.g., <u>nausea</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <br>Targeted DMARDs (<u>JAK inhibitors</u>)<br> | <br>* <u>Tofacitinib</u> DOSAGE or <u>baricitinib</u> DOSAGE: second-line treatment<br><br> | <br>* Adverse effects<br><br>* Severe infections<br><br>* <u>TB</u> reactivation<br><br>* <u>Anemia</u> [[30]](/library/2acTPa0)<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Methotrexate</u> monotherapy is strongly recommended over all other synthetic and <u>biologic DMARDs</u> in patients with moderate to high disease activity. [[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)




##### <u>Biologic DMARDs</u> [[30]](/library/2acTPa0)




* Indication: : persistent moderate or severe disease activity after 3 months of <u>conventional DMARD</u> therapy

* Agents

* <u>TNF-α inhibitors</u>: e.g., <u>adalimumab</u> DOSAGE, <u>infliximab</u> DOSAGE, <u>etanercept</u> DOSAGE (see also “<u>Contraindications to anti-TNF-α treatment</u>”)

* Others: <u>rituximab</u>, <u>anakinra</u>, <u>tocilizumab</u>

* Adverse effects include:

* Infections

* <u>TB</u> reactivation

* <u>Hepatitis B</u> reactivation





> [!TIP]
> All <u>biologic DMARDs</u> have similar <u>efficacy</u> when combined with <u>MTX</u>. When choosing a biologic <u>DMARD</u>, consider patient preferences, comorbidities, potential adverse effects, and drug availability. [[7]](/library/eacxja0)




##### Prevention and monitoring of adverse effects [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[35]](/library/AdcRsY0)[[37]](/library/XpY9LJ)[[38]](/library/KbcUua0)




Perform studies and <u>vaccinations</u> before the initiation of therapy based on the patient's individual risk and potential adverse effects of the prospective agent.




* <u>CBC</u>, <u>liver</u> <u>transaminases</u>, and serum <u>creatinine</u> at baseline

* <u>HCV</u> and <u>HBV serology</u> at baseline

* <u>TB</u> screening (see “Diagnosis of <u>latent TB</u>”): Perform baseline screening in patients who will receive <u>biologic DMARDs</u> or <u>tofacitinib</u>.

* <u>Vaccinations</u> for patients receiving <u>biologic DMARDs</u>

* <u>Influenza</u>, <u>pneumococcus</u>, and <u>hepatitis B</u>

* <u>Herpes zoster</u>

* Offer <u>contraception counseling</u>, <u>family planning</u>, and information on <u>teratogenicity</u> of pharmacological treatment to all patients. See also “<u>RA</u> in <u>pregnancy</u>.”





### Nonpharmacological management  [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)




* <u>ASCVD prevention</u> measures  are associated with improved outcomes in patients with <u>RA</u>.

* Physical and <u>occupational therapy</u> can improve mobility.

* Heat or cold packs for <u>pain management</u>.





### Surgical treatment [[25]](/library/KZcUca0)[[39]](/library/RXclBa0)




* Indications

* Consider in patients with extensive <u>joint</u> deformity.

* Rarely, <u>surgery</u> may be used for symptom control in patients who do not respond to or cannot tolerate the recommended pharmacological regimen.

* Procedures

* <u>Total joint replacement</u> (e.g., <u>hip joint replacement</u>): Consider in patients with severe <u>joint</u> damage or concomitant <u>osteoarthritis</u>.

* Synovectomy: surgical removal of the synovial tissue

* Radiation synovectomy: <u>ablation</u> of inflamed <u>synovia</u> via injection of radioactive agents (beta particles) into the synovial cavity of affected <u>joints</u> [[40]](/library/hVcc8Y0)

* Inhibits synovial growth and <u>fibrosis</u> of the <u>synovia</u>

* May reduce inflammatory activity and <u>pain</u>

* Also indicated in patients with other chronic inflammatory <u>joint</u> diseases (e.g., active arthrosis, <u>psoriatic arthritis</u>) who do not respond to pharmacological treatment

## Classification

The <u>ACR</u>/<u>EULAR</u> classification criteria were developed for research purposes and should not be used as diagnostic criteria. These criteria are for targeted use in patients who have at least one <u>joint</u> with clinical <u>synovitis</u> that is not better explained by another cause, e.g. trauma or degenerative <u>joint</u> conditions.  [[24]](/library/s5atlO)




| <br>2010 <u>ACR</u>/<u>EULAR</u> criteria for the classification of <u>RA</u> [[24]](/library/s5atlO)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Score | <br><u>Joint</u> involvement (<u>pain</u> or swelling)<br> | <br><u>Serology</u><br> | <br><u>Acute-phase reactants</u><br> | Symptom duration |
| 0 | <br>≤ 1 <u>large joint</u><br> | Negative RF and <u>ACPA</u><br> | Normal <u>CRP</u> and <u>ESR</u><br> | < 6 weeks |
| 1 | <br>2–10 <u>large joints</u><br> | – | <br>↑ <u>CRP</u> or <u>ESR</u><br> | ≥ 6 weeks |
| 2 | <br>1–3 <u>small joints</u> (with or without <u>large joint</u> involvement) | Low positive  RF or <u>ACPA</u><br> | – | – |
| 3 | <br>4–10 <u>small joints</u> (with or without <u>large joint</u> involvement) | High positive  RF or <u>ACPA</u><br> | – | – |
| 5 | <br>> 10 <u>joints</u> (including at least one <u>small joint</u>) | – | – | – |
| <br>Score: Obtained by adding together the points from each feature  Interpretation: <br><br>* Patients with a score of ≥ 6 points fulfill the <u>RA</u> classification criteria.<br><br>* Patients who do not fulfill the classification criteria can still be diagnosed with <u>RA</u> at the clinician's discretion.  [[24]](/library/s5atlO)[[25]](/library/KZcUca0)<br><br><br><br> |  |  |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> The <u>ACR</u>/<u>EULAR</u> classification criteria have high <u>specificity</u> but low <u>sensitivity</u>. Therefore, the purpose of these criteria is to standardize case definitions for enrollment in clinical studies, not to guide practice. [[7]](/library/eacxja0)[[24]](/library/s5atlO)[[41]](/library/LwbwjD)

## Complications

Untreated and/or severe cases can result in permanent damage to the <u>joints</u> with stiffening and deformity.




* Complications in the upper limbs: <u>rheumatoid hand</u> deformities (see “Clinical features” above)

* Complications in the lower limbs

* <u>Baker cyst</u> due to inflammatory <u>joint effusion</u>

* Foot impairment: pes plano‑valgus (<u>flat feet</u>)  [[42]](/library/ZMaZMO)

* Other complications

* <u>Muscle weakness</u>

* <u>Vasculitis</u> involving the <u>kidneys</u>

* <u>Amyloid</u> A <u>amyloidosis</u> (<u>AA amyloidosis</u>)

* <u>Septic arthritis</u>  [[43]](/library/YManMO)

* <u>Osteopenia</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>, and bone <u>fractures</u>  [[44]](/library/cMaanO)

* <u>Caplan syndrome</u>





![Popliteal (Baker) cyst](media/ub4irpde8xztrvvzzs2l93eh.jpg)

Popliteal (Baker) cyst




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prognosis

* Factors associated with poor prognosis

* Cardiovascular disease and infections are the most common <u>causes of death</u>. [[12]](/library/TYa6oQ)

* Male sex [[45]](/library/5qbi_u)

* Smoking

* Social factors (e.g., low <u>socioeconomic status</u>, low level of education)

* Presence of extraarticular disease

* Elevated <u>laboratory values</u> associated with poor prognosis

* <u>CRP</u>

* <u>ESR</u>

* <u>ACPA</u>

* RF

---
